_doc: Fleet-baseline deny rails, keyed by channel mount — the centralized half of the gating engine (agent-core design, 2026-07-13, chunk B). Shipped with the canopy plugin so a rail fix propagates to every agent via /canopy:update. Each agent's hooks/gating_guard.py reads its config/gating.json `channels` list, pulls these rails for the mounted channels, substitutes {slug}, and merges them IN FRONT of the repo's own `deny` list at call time. ADD-ONLY: an agent's local config can add rails; it can never remove a baseline rail. Rails here must stay channel-generic — agent-specific rails belong in that agent's config/gating.json.
_always_doc: Rails that apply to EVERY agent regardless of which channels it mounts, because what they govern is not a channel. Gated per-agent by `requires_path` instead — the rail applies only where the file it protects actually exists. A channel home would mean each agent opting in via its own gating.json, i.e. the rail is missing for precisely the agent that forgot, which is the failure being fixed.

always._pattern_doc: The pre-send review wrapper collision. An agent that ships skills/agent-turn-review/ owns a NAMESPACED wrapper ({slug}:agent-turn-review) carrying its own send path, its done-claim rules and its gates; the fleet skill (canopy:agent-turn-review) is the BODY that wrapper delegates to. Calling the body directly, or the bare name, satisfies the letter of 'run the review' while silently skipping every agent-specific step — the wrapper's own words: 'a wrapper you can walk around is not a wrapper.' Measured 2026-08-27 by `canopy agent-review`. hal's wrapper PREDICTED the bypass in prose in its own opening paragraph and was bypassed anyway. The source was upstream: this plugin's own agent-turn-review SKILL.md told adopters to write 'invoke canopy:agent-turn-review', and src/orchestrator/agent_factory.py stamped it, so echo/eva/ada were each BORN instructing the agent to call the body and skip its own wrapper. ACE caught it independently and refused to follow that instruction. Both halves were prose asking the model to comply, and both failed, which is this repo's standing argument for a rail. Matches the `skill` argument exactly, so a wrapper's own {slug}: name is never touched. deny, never ask: an 'ask' is a blocking modal that stalls autonomous work.
always.message: BLOCKED: `agent-turn-review` bare / `canopy:agent-turn-review` is the fleet BODY, not the entry point. Invoke `{slug}:agent-turn-review` — the wrapper this repo ships — which runs the same fleet discipline AND {slug}'s own send path, done-claim rules and gates. Calling the body directly passes the checklist while skipping all of those. A wrapper you can walk around is not a wrapper.

always._pattern_doc: Scratch-worktree collisions. Agents stand up throwaway worktrees constantly (deploying a clean origin/main, grounding a finding in a sibling repo, checking CI gates elsewhere), and the skills that teach it hand out a FIXED path -- hal's skills/turn taught `worktree add /tmp/canopy-main` in the one procedure it repeats most, so every derived invention (/tmp/canopy-win, /tmp/canopy-harvest, /tmp/cl-1427) inherited the shape. Two sessions of the same agent run concurrently as a matter of course, so a fixed name is a collision waiting for the second one. Measured 2026-09-04 by `canopy agent-review hal`: three failures in one 6h window across two sessions -- `'/tmp/canopy-win' is a missing but already registered worktree`, `'hal/windows-text-encoding' is already used by worktree at '/private/tmp/canopy-win'`, and `a branch named 'hal/windows-text-encoding' already exists`. Same day, that repo carried 15 abandoned /tmp/canopy-* worktrees, all merged and clean, one still holding the branch a later session then failed to create. `mktemp -d` removes the whole class in one token. Matches only a LITERAL /tmp path, so `"$WT"`, `$(mktemp -d)` and mktemp's own /tmp/tmp.XXXXXX pass untouched; named homes outside /tmp (~/emdash/worktrees/...) are deliberately out of scope -- they are a workspace convention, not scratch. `always`, not a channel: every agent does this, so a per-channel opt-in would leave the rail missing for exactly the agent that forgot.
always.message:
BLOCKED: `git worktree add` at a fixed /tmp path. Two {slug} sessions run at once, so a name you picked collides -- as `already exists`, as `missing but already registered worktree` once /tmp is cleaned under the registration, or as `<branch> is already used by worktree at <other path>`. Use a unique one and remove it on the way out:
  WT=$(mktemp -d)
  git -C "$REPO" worktree prune
  git -C "$REPO" worktree add "$WT" origin/main --detach
  ... work ...
  git -C "$REPO" worktree remove --force "$WT"
Use --detach whenever you are only READING a ref -- checking out a branch takes it hostage from every other worktree. If you genuinely need a branch, make its NAME unique too; `worktree prune` never reclaims a worktree whose directory still exists.

always._bash_only_doc: A `"tool": "Bash"` rail covers every shell tool (the engine's SHELL_TOOLS), because nearly every rail is about the COMMAND. This one is about the SHELL: EQUALS expansion is zsh behaviour, and in PowerShell `echo =====` just prints. Applying it there would block a harmless command for a reason that is false on that shell.
always._pattern_doc: zsh EQUALS expansion. With EQUALS on (zsh's default; zsh is the shell the Bash tool runs on macOS), a word that starts with an unquoted `=` is replaced by the path of the command named by the rest of the word, and a lookup miss is fatal to the WHOLE line. So the separator agents reach for between two reads -- `echo =====` -- asks zsh for a command called `====`: `(eval):1: ==== not found`, every statement after it skipped, Exit code 1. The agent sees the output of the statements BEFORE the separator plus a bare exit 1, and blames the wrong statement: `canopy agent-review hal` diagnosed exactly this as 'head/tail pipes report exit 1' when the pipes were innocent. Measured 2026-09-11 over 7 days of fleet transcripts (27k Bash calls): 41 such tool results in 15 sessions across ace, eva, ada and hal, none a `[ a == b ]` test. Matches an echo/printf statement (at statement start, or after then/do/else -- one of the 41 was a `for ...; do echo =====` loop) whose FIRST non-flag argument is a bare `=` followed by more characters. That shape is all 41. It deliberately stops there: following quoting past the first argument (to also catch `printf '%s\n' ===`) caught nothing more in the same corpus and fired on legitimate commands -- escaped quotes (`'...'\''...'`) and `$(... "..." ...)` inside double quotes. A `(` / `{` prefix was dropped for the same reason: it caught nothing and fired on a quoted `--title "... (echo ===)"`. Everything else passes: quoted ('===', "==="), escaped (\===), mid-word (a=b, --format=x), a lone `=` (zsh leaves it alone), and `==` outside echo/printf ([[ $a == b ]], awk '$1 == 2', python3 -c "x == y", A=b). Known over-match: the statement split ignores quoting, so `echo ===` inside a remote `sh -c '...'` (3 calls in the corpus, harmless there) or a heredoc line is blocked too -- quoting it costs nothing. `always`, not a channel: every agent shares the shell.
always.message:
BLOCKED: `echo`/`printf` with an argument starting with an unquoted `=`. {slug}'s Bash runs under zsh, where EQUALS expansion reads `=foo` as "the path of command foo" -- so `echo =====` looks up a command named `====`, dies with `(eval):1: ==== not found`, and aborts the WHOLE line: the statements before it print, the ones after it never run, and the call returns Exit code 1 for a reason that has nothing to do with them. Quote the separator:
  echo '====='
(or use `echo -----`). A lone `=` and `=` mid-word (a=b) are fine unquoted.

always._pattern_doc: Raw `aws sso login` from an agent turn. Before 2026-10-09 the only fix for an expired AWS SSO session was a human at that box's terminal, so agents learned to stop and ask for it. Alarm turns stalled for hours on that ask: today's canopy-web 5xx turn, and a board task blocked for 1-2 days in late September. `canopy aws login` (canopy-web#1374) runs the device-code flow and pushes a tap-to-approve alert to the runner owner's phone, and the alert says who is asking, on which runner, and why. A raw `aws sso login` in an agent turn either tries to open a browser on a headless box or prints a link into a transcript nobody is reading, and either way it waits for a human who has not been told. Prose could not carry this: the old instruction lived in a dozen per-agent skill lines and fix strings, and an agent that has never read them still reaches for the AWS CLI's own advice. Matches `aws sso login` at the start of a statement, including after an env prefix (AWS_PROFILE=labs aws sso login) and after then/do/else. `--help` passes. The remedy itself (`canopy aws login`) does not match, because it has no `sso`. It spawns `aws sso login` as a subprocess, which no hook sees. A quoted mention (grep "aws sso login") is not at statement start and also passes. `aws configure sso` (first-time profile setup) is a different verb and passes. A human who really wants the terminal flow types it with `!`, which runs outside the hook. `always`, not a channel: AWS is not a channel, and any agent on a runner can hit it.
always.message:
BLOCKED: raw `aws sso login` waits for a human who has not been told. Run instead:
  canopy aws login --profile <profile> --reason "<one line: what you need AWS for>"
with run_in_background (or a 10-minute Bash timeout), and keep doing the work that needs no AWS while it waits. It pushes a tap-to-approve alert to this runner owner's phone saying that {slug} is asking, on which runner, and your reason, then finishes by itself once they approve. The reason is required and is what they read on the lock screen, so make it specific ("confirm the canopy-web 5xx cause in /ecs/labs-jj-canopy-web", not "need AWS"). If it prints "could not push", deliver the link it printed to the owner. If it times out, say in one line that AWS is the blocker.

always._pattern_doc: PowerShell's own HTTP-write spellings. Shell rails now apply to PowerShell too (the engine treats `"tool": "Bash"` as every shell), which covers `gog …`, `canopy …` and `curl.exe -X POST …` because those are spelled the same in both shells. It does NOT cover PowerShell's native cmdlets: every agent's HTTP-write rail is written in curl form (e.g. a Salesforce `curl -X POST`), so `Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post` reaches the same endpoint past all of them. Found 2026-09-22 by Shayoni Mazumdar on fizzy. One translation rail here instead of a PowerShell twin of every curl rail in every agent, which would drift the first time someone added a rail and forgot its twin -- the same reasoning as her local stopgap. Matches Invoke-RestMethod / Invoke-WebRequest and their irm / iwr aliases with a non-GET -Method (PowerShell accepts any unique parameter prefix, so -Me / -Meth / -Method:Post all count) or with -CustomMethod. Reads (no -Method, or -Method Get/Head/Options) pass: reads run free.
always.message: BLOCKED: `Invoke-RestMethod` / `Invoke-WebRequest` with a write method. {slug}'s HTTP rails are written against `curl`, so this cmdlet would reach the same endpoint past every one of them. Send it as `curl.exe -X <METHOD> …` (or through the Bash tool) so the rails can see it. Reads — no -Method, or -Method Get — are not affected.

email.message: BLOCKED: raw `gog gmail send/reply` bypasses {slug}'s HTML wrapper and thread_id capture. Send via bin/{slug}-email (the shared canopy email engine) instead — write the body to a file and pass --body-file.

BLOCKED: `canopy email send --account` overrides {slug}'s repo identity — one mailbox per agent, never shared (identity bleed is the fleet's one hard rule). Send via bin/{slug}-email, which pins this repo's identity.

gws._pattern_doc: Deliverable filing rail for the RAW gog path (agent-core/deliverables.md rule 1). BROADENED 2026-08-13: this used to fire only on `gog drive upload --convert`, and each agent hand-added its own extra verbs locally — so the enforced set was a short, per-agent list of the creation commands somebody had thought of. `gog sheets create` was in nobody's list, and on 2026-08-12 Eva built a 45-row target roster with it straight into her My Drive root, unshared. A denylist of verbs always trails the tool surface, so this now matches the SHAPE — any gog subcommand that creates a Drive object — and requires a destination. `--help` is exempted so the rail can't stop you reading the command's own usage `--replace` is exempted too (2026-10-07): `drive upload --replace <id>` overwrites an existing file in its existing home and creates nothing — and gog REJECTS `--parent` alongside it, so the rail used to make an in-place replace impossible to run at all.
gws.message: BLOCKED: {slug} never creates a Google Doc / Sheet / Slide / folder in My Drive root — it is invisible to the team, a dead link to @dimagi.com recipients, and it dies with the agent identity. Pass `--parent <folderId>` under {slug}'s OWN root. Resolve the destination instead of pasting an id: `canopy gdoc publish --project "<Project>"` (markdown → Doc) or `canopy gsheet publish --project "<Project>"` (TSV/CSV → Sheet) both find-or-create <root>/Projects/<Project>, file, share and verify in one call; `--area "Process State"` for a durable tracker. SEARCH FIRST — reuse the project's existing folder rather than spawning a parallel one. See agent-core/deliverables.md.

gws._pattern_doc: Same rail for the canopy publishing engines. Without a destination flag `publish` falls back to the agent's Drive ROOT, i.e. beside Projects/ rather than inside it — the mistake deliverables.md rule 1 names explicitly. `--replace` is exempt (it keeps the existing doc's home) and so is `--help`: before 2026-08-13 this rail matched `canopy gdoc publish --help`, so an agent could not read the usage of the command it was being told to use.
gws.message: BLOCKED: `canopy gdoc/gsheet/gslides publish` with no destination files into {slug}'s Drive ROOT, beside Projects/ instead of inside it. Pass `--project "<Project>"` (a per-project subfolder, find-or-create, reused across turns), `--area "Process State"` for a durable tracker, or `--replace <id>` to update an existing artifact in place. See agent-core/deliverables.md.

gws._pattern_doc: The MCP half of the same rail, added 2026-08-13. Every rail above is `tool: Bash`, so an agent holding a Drive-creating MCP tool (chrome-sales gdrive, ace-gdrive) could file anywhere with nothing to stop it — the Bash path was railed while the richer path beside it was wide open. Matched on tool NAME shape via `tool_pattern`, because the same creator carries a different plugin mount per agent. The pattern then tests the tool's ARGUMENTS (the hook JSON-serializes MCP input) for any of the parent/folder keys these servers use; absent all of them, the object lands in My Drive root. `sheets_create` is negative-lookahead'd against `_tab` on purpose: `sheets_create_tab` adds a worksheet INSIDE an existing spreadsheet, creates no Drive object, and takes a spreadsheetId rather than a parent — so the rail had no satisfiable form and simply blocked a legitimate operation forever. Found 2026-08-26, when an agent wanting a Notes tab on a sheet it already owned was told to pass a parent argument the tool does not have, and worked around it by writing into spare columns instead.
gws.message: BLOCKED: that MCP call creates a Drive object with no destination, which lands it in {slug}'s My Drive root — invisible to the team and dead-linked to @dimagi.com recipients. Pass the server's parent/folder argument, pointing at a per-project subfolder under {slug}'s OWN root. Easier: `canopy gdoc publish --project "<Project>"` / `canopy gsheet publish --project "<Project>"` resolve, file, share and verify in one call. See agent-core/deliverables.md.

gws._pattern_doc: `gog docs` WRITE verbs invoked with `--dry-run` / `-n`. THE FLAG IS A LIE: on gog v0.12.0 `--dry-run` on `gog docs insert|delete|find-replace|update|edit|sed|write|clear` prints the intended action AND PERFORMS IT. Verified 2026-08-26 on a throwaway doc: `gog docs insert <id> "ZULU" --index 1 --dry-run` printed `inserted 4 bytes` and the document then began `ZULU`; the same held for `delete` (4 characters really removed) and `find-replace` (the replacement really applied). Reads (`cat`, `export`, `info`, `structure`, `list-tabs`) are unaffected and are NOT matched. WHY THIS IS A RAIL AND NOT A NOTE: `--dry-run` is precisely the flag an agent reaches for in order to be SAFE, so the failure lands on the most careful turn, not the sloppiest -- and it is silent, because the printed output is indistinguishable from a real dry run. It cost a real deliverable on 2026-08-26: a dry-run + real-run pair on the UNGA 2026 planning doc applied twice each time -- the bullet was inserted twice, and the follow-up `delete` of the 998-char duplicate ran twice and took the next 998 chars with it, destroying the 'Target outreach list' HEADING_1, its intro, the status-values line, the 'Added for UNGA 2026' HEADING_2, the whole Navyn Salem entry and most of Ron Dalgliesh. Recovered only because the turn happened to hold a full `gog docs cat` capture from before the edit. ANCHORED to a real invocation (command start or after a shell separator) so prose and commit messages that quote the command do not trip it -- the calendar-delete rail paid for that lesson three times in two days. Both lookaheads are order-independent, so the flag is caught before or after the verb. Promoted from eva's local config to the fleet baseline 2026-10-04 (it is a property of gog, not of eva). Pinned by tests/test_gating_baseline_gog_docs_dry_run.py. Verified on gog v0.12.0; not re-tested on 0.38.1 — the rail costs nothing if the flag was since fixed (the write without it is the path the message teaches), so re-verify on a throwaway doc before REMOVING it, not before keeping it.
gws.message: BLOCKED: `gog docs` has no working dry run -- on gog v0.12.0 `--dry-run` PERFORMS the write and prints it as if it were hypothetical (verified for insert, delete and find-replace). A dry-run-then-run pair therefore applies TWICE; on 2026-08-26 that silently destroyed a section of a live planning doc. THE RIGHT PATH: (1) capture the current text first -- `gog docs cat <id> -a <acct> > "$WD/before.txt"` (WD=$(mktemp -d)) -- so any mistake is recoverable; (2) get exact indices from `gog docs structure <id> -a <acct> --json` (a READ, safe); (3) make the change ONCE, with no dry-run flag, and verify by re-reading. For anything index-based or multi-step, send ONE Docs API batch as yourself -- `gog api call docs v1 documents.batchUpdate --params '{"documentId":"<id>"}' --body '{"requests":[...]}' --allow-write --force -a <acct> --client <client> --json` -- which executes exactly once and is atomic across requests. Then `canopy gdoc check <id>`. Reads (`cat`, `export`, `info`, `structure`, `list-tabs`) are unaffected -- this rail does not match them.
